For the people, by the peephole

It is common wisdom among journalists that, to ensure that a lead covers all the main points of a story, one must follow the five ‘Ws’: who, where, why, and what the hell were you thinking when you started this? I merged the last two for convenience.

Given that this starts feeling much like an opinion piece on a provincial newspaper, I will abide by journalists’ golden in introducong what I have pompously decided to call – but I am quite sure I will backtrack on it – Policy Unmaking.

Who am I, but above all who are you?

Who is but the form following the function of what, and what I am is a bored researcher. It is not that I have nothing to do, but I have very little motivation to do what I ought to do at the moment. I have spent my adult life so far wrapping my head around policymaking and how it occurs - in all fairness, with modest results - and I feel like it has not been time well spent.

About me, I like Pina Coladas and getting caught in the rain, but what I am really keen on is sarcasm. I am fluent in cynicism and and I guess wordplay in titles are the only salvageable part of my academic work.

But then, who are you, you on the other side of the barricade? Most likely, at this point, no one. If this takes off, you will be probably a few friends and family. But who is this actually addressed to?

In my delusional fantasies, the people. Yes the people, the ones who get to experience policy as ramblings of bureaucrats in a dull meeting room in Brussels, deciding how plastic bottle caps shall be shaped.

This newsletter is for you, to make you realise that that’s exactly what policymaking is. But also, perhaps, that there’s more to the story.

Boredom and an unjustified burst of self-confidence

We skip the where, because if anyone’s going to read this, it would be redundant. So, why then? Mainly, because I am stuck with my writing and decided - following what I realised is a common pattern in my life - to address the issue by focusing on something else. I learned from a reel that this might have to do with my APhD, which is has the same symptoms of ADHD and other trendy neurodivergencies, but we know its cause: poor-judgement in your career choices.

Anyways, if that is the reason, I could have just kept a journal. I tried, with little success. There is, thus, a deeper, more annoying itch that brought me here and it is the latent fear that all I have been doing in the past four years is going to end up in a pile (well, metaphorically, we are all paper-free nowadays) of scrap.

So, we get to the what.

What the hell I was thinking when I started this

Bear with me for a second. What I do as a researcher is to go to people with a set of assumptions about how policy is being made, the reason they do what they do. And I watch those assumption crumble, question after question. So, I go back to reflect on my failures, and I read, read, and read again about all the interesting things very smart people have written over the past decades. I work out a couple of slightly sharper, brand-new interpretations, I get face to face with my interviewees and watch them proving me wrong again. So, I roll up my sleeves and… well, you get it at this point.

A reasonable person would note that this is a pointless exercise. And it probably is. But, if anything, I now have a bunch of wrong theories and assumptions about how policies are made. And that’s my what, what I would like to talk about in this substack if I actually manage to get through the ‘fresh start enthusiasm lock-in threshold’, as I like to call it. What is left out of papers and books, but is essential to understand how policy works in practice.

I want this to be a space where to discuss research findings, mine and others’. Half a news digest, half a research journal to put theories to work in the analysis of everyday policy making, in the EU and elsewhere. Unmaking assumptions, decostructing narratives, and peeking at power in policy through the peephole of policy studies.
